absaetze.t: In der zweiten Heimat des Papstes, Peru, gibt es Missbrauchsvorwürfe gegen Sodalicio - eine Organisation, die trotz Verbots noch Einfluss hat. Für dieses Verbot spielte Papst Leo eine entscheidende Rolle.

Am Tag, als Papst Leo der Vierzehnte seine Südamerika-Reise startete, rückten in seiner Wahlheimat Peru erneut Missbrauchsvorwürfe in den Fokus: 77 Geistliche wurden in den vergangenen Jahren öffentlich des Missbrauchs beschuldigt.

Anne Barret-Doyle vom US-Portal Bishop Accountability erklärte gegenüber Journalisten: "Wir glauben, dass 77 nur ein winziger Bruchteil der tatsächlichen Zahl ist und dass sich in diesem Land noch Tausende von Opfern zu Wort melden müssen."
Sodalicio - die Soldaten Christi

Der erste, der sich in Peru zu Wort meldete, war Jose Escardó. Er war 17 Jahre alt, als er beschloss, ein sogenannter Soldat Christi zu werden - und Sodalicio beizutreten. Die ultrarechte katholische Laienbewegung verstand sich damals, 1977, als Gegenbewegung zur linken Befreiungstheologie in Lateinamerika.

Wir wollten die Welt verbessern, sagt er heute per Videocall, doch wir wurden missbraucht. "Sie nannten es ‚Anforderungen‘, denn - so hieß es - wir müssten unzerstörbar sein, geistig, körperlich und emotional. Man befahl uns, einander in Gesicht und Magen zu schlagen, bis der erste zu Boden ging", sagt Escardó.

Und: "Auf der Treppe zu schlafen, uns mit schmutzigem Toilettenwasser das Gesicht waschen - abgesehen von der sexuellen Gewalt, die einige von uns, wie ich, erlitten haben." Er beschuldigte Sodalicio bereits im Jahr 2000 des Missbrauchs, wurde daraufhin jahrelang bedroht. Erst 15 Jahre später kam Bewegung in den Fall.

Bewegung auch durch eine umfassende Recherche der zwei Journalisten Pedro Salinas und Paola Ugaz zu den düsteren Machenschaften der Organisation, die Escardó als kriminelles Netzwerk beschreibt. Diese reichten von sexuellen Übergriffen und Machtmissbrauch bis zu Landraub und illegalen Finanzgeschäften.
Erst 2025 aufgelöst

2025 wurde die Sodalicio-Bewegung von Papst Franziskus aufgelöst, und dabei spielte der Bischof von Chiclayo eine entscheidende Rolle, sagt Escardó. Der Bischof heißt Robert Prevost, heute Papst Leo XIV. Er hat fast 21 Jahre - zuerst als Missionar, dann als Bischof - in Peru gearbeitet, besitzt sogar die Staatsangehörigkeit.

Umso größer war die Hoffnung, dass es während seines Besuchs nun zu einem Treffen mit Sodalicio-Opfern kommen könnte. Doch daran hätten die Organisatoren der Reise kein Interesse, glaubt Escardó, heute Vorsitzender der Missbrauchsopfer Perus. "Wir, eine Gruppe von 33 Betroffenen, haben einen offenen Brief an den Papst unterzeichnet. Das Anliegen, dass er nicht nur mit den Opfern zusammentrifft, sondern erfährt, dass der Prozess zur Auflösung des Sodalicio nicht abgeschlossen ist", sagt Escardó.

"Es gibt keine Gerechtigkeit, keine Wiedergutmachung und keine Heilung für die Opfer; und es fehlen jegliche Schutz- und Präventionsmaßnahmen." Dass sich Leo während seiner Zeit als Bischof für die Auflösung von Sodalicio stark gemacht hat, brachte ihm nicht nur Freunde. Dass vor dem Konklave Anschuldigungen kursierten, Prevost habe selbst Missbrauchsvorwürfe vertuscht - diese Anschuldigungen widerlegen inzwischen zahlreiche Recherchen. Escardó sieht es als Rachefeldzug.
Nach wie vor großer Einfluss
Nach wie vor verfügten mit Sodalicio verbundene Persönlichkeiten über großen Einfluss in Peru - auch in der Bischofskonferenz, welche die Reise von Papst Leo mitorganisiert hat.

Das beobachtet auch Paola Ugaz, eine der beiden Journalistinnen, die den Fall mit aufrollten. "Ich glaube, die Absicht derjenigen, die diese Reise organisieren, ist genau das: Sie demonstrieren, dass sie weiter die Oberhand haben, dass sie nie weg waren. Und deswegen werden jetzt keine Wellen schlagen. Den Fall Sodalicio wurde hier in Peru einfach unter den Teppich gekehrt."

Papst Leo hat sich in Argentinien mit Missbrauchsopfern getroffen - darunter sind keine Vertreter der Gruppen, die explizit um ein Treffen gebeten hatten. Die Auswahl sei intransparent. Es könne nicht sein, dass Repräsentanten der Kirche, und damit im Grunde ja von der Täterorganisation, allein entscheiden, wer am Treffen teilnimmt, kritisiert Escardó.
Große Aufgabe für die katholische Kirche

Die argentinische Soziologin Ana Lourdes, die über Missbrauch und Machtstrukturen in der katholischen Kirche Lateinamerikas forscht, sagt dennoch: Es sei ein Wandel erkennbar. "Ein Wandel hat eingesetzt - oder besser gesagt: Der Moment des Wandels ist gekommen –, in dem die Kirche den Opfern Glauben schenkt und Empathie sowie Mitgefühl für sie empfindet." Papst Leo nehme eine solche Haltung ein. "Er signalisiert: ‚Es ist mir wichtig.‘ Das hat einen symbolischen Wert."

Dennoch bleibe er Teil eines Getriebes, in dem Missbrauch ein systemisches und strukturelles Problem sei. "Es gibt nach wie vor sehr viel Vertuschung. Der Schutz der Kirche hatte Vorrang vor dem Schutz der Opfer. Es ist eine Illusion zu glauben, dass es vorbei ist."

In Argentinien ließ Leo durchscheinen, dass ihm durchaus bewusst ist, vor welcher großen Aufgabe die Kirche steht - und wie das Thema Missbrauch auch das Vertrauen in die Institution untergraben hat. In Buenos Aires rief er auch die Menschen zurück zum Gebet, die von Menschen verletzt wurden, die sie eigentlich hätten begleiten sollen.

items.titel: Historischer Sieg: Demokrat Colom holt Senatssitz in Mississippi
items.anriss: Erstmals seit mehr als vier Jahrzehnten hat ein Demokrat im südlichen US-Bundesstaat Mississippi eine Wahl für den US-Senat gewonnen. Colom gelang ein überraschender Sieg - er weitet damit die Mehrheit im Senat ab Januar auf 55 der 100 …

absaetze.t: Erstmals seit mehr als vier Jahrzehnten hat ein Demokrat im südlichen US-Bundesstaat Mississippi eine Wahl für den US-Senat gewonnen. Colom gelang ein überraschender Sieg - er weitet damit die Mehrheit im Senat ab Januar auf 55 der 100 Sitze aus.

Der demokratische Kandidat Scott Colom hat sich nach einer langwierigen Stimmenauszählung in dem hart umkämpften Rennen um einen Sitz im US-Senat in Mississippi durchgesetzt. Gegen die republikanische Senatorin Cindy Hyde-Smith ist der knappe Sieg eine Überraschung für Mississippi, das seit Generationen größtenteils von den konservativen Republikanern kontrolliert wurde.

Die Nachrichtenagentur Associated Press (AP) erklärte den 43-jährigen Staatsanwalt Colom am Mittwoch zum Sieger, nachdem die lokalen Wahlbeamten mehrere Tage lang Briefwahl- und vorläufige Stimmzettel, in Mississippi sogenannte Affidavit-Stimmzettel, ausgewertet hatten.

Die republikanische Senatorin Hyde-Smith gestand die Niederlage bereits ein: "Auch wenn dies nicht das Ergebnis ist, auf das wir hingearbeitet oder auf das wir gehofft haben, respektiere ich die Entscheidung der Wählerinnen und Wähler in Mississippi", sagte sie in einem auf X geteilten Video. "Ich möchte Scott Colom gratulieren und ihm alles Gute für die große Verantwortung wünschen, die er nun übernimmt - unseren großartigen Bundesstaat zu vertreten."

Der Bundesstaat hat mit knapp 37 Prozent der Bevölkerung den höchsten Anteil Schwarzer. Trotzdem gab es seit über einem Jahrhundert keinen schwarzen US-Senator mehr aus dem Bundesstaat. 1875 zog der zuvor versklavte Blanche Kelso Bruce für den Bundesstaat in den US-Senat ein und absolvierte als erster Afroamerikaner eine volle Amtszeit in der Parlamentskammer.

"Sie verdienen tatsächlich einen Senator, der ihnen zuhört, der sich wirklich dafür interessiert, was sie denken, und der sich wirklich darum kümmert, was sie gerade durchmachen", sagte Colom in der Schlussphase des Wahlkampfs.
Kritik an Trumps Kurs
Ausschlaggebend waren unter anderem die hohe Zahl schwarzer Wähler, Unzufriedenheit mit der wirtschaftlichen Lage und Fehler seiner Konkurrentin im Wahlkampf.

Coloms Sieg ist Teil einer Reihe von Niederlagen der Republikaner bei den Zwischenwahlen und gilt als Rückschlag für US-Präsident Donald Trump und seine Partei. Zugleich sehen Demokraten darin ein Zeichen, dass sie auch im traditionell konservativen Süden der USA Erfolge erzielen können.

Colom hatte im Wahlkampf unter anderem Trumps Iran-Politik und die Zölle kritisiert, zugleich aber persönliche Angriffe auf den Präsidenten und dessen Wähler vermieden. Er kündigte an, sich für die Interessen aller Einwohner Mississippis einsetzen zu wollen.

Damit weiten die Demokraten ihre Mehrheit im Senat ab Januar auf 55 der 100 Sitze aus. Offen ist zudem weiter das Rennen in Alaska, bei dem die demokratische Kandidatin Mary Peltola aktuell knapp in Führung liegt.

items.titel: Les démocrates prennent un nouveau siège aux républicains, au sénat américain
items.anriss: Le démocrate Scott Colom est parvenu à prendre aux républicains un siège au Sénat américain dans le Mississippi, lors des élections de mi-mandat, selon les projections de médias mercredi. Il est le premier sénateur noir à être élu en près …

absaetze.t: Le démocrate Scott Colom est parvenu à prendre aux républicains un siège au Sénat américain dans le Mississippi, lors des élections de mi-mandat, selon les projections de médias mercredi. Il est le premier sénateur noir à être élu en près de 150 ans dans cet Etat.
Il s'agit d'une percée spectaculaire dans cet Etat du sud des Etats-Unis traditionnellement conservateur. Scott Colom va devenir le premier sénateur démocrate du Mississippi depuis 1989.

Ce procureur de district de 43 ans a vaincu la sénatrice républicaine sortante, Cindy Hyde-Smith, à l'issue des élections de mi-mandat au cours desquelles les démocrates ont repris la majorité dans les deux chambres du Congrès.
>> Lire à ce sujet : Les résultats détaillés des élections de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis
Au moins 55 sièges démocrates au sénat

Son succès, annoncé par plusieurs médias américains, tels que CNN, NBC et CBS, va permettre aux démocrates de bénéficier d'au moins 55 des 100 sièges au Sénat. Les républicains en ont obtenu 44, tandis qu'en Alaska, le dépouillement est toujours en cours.
Il donne, jeudi matin, 49% des voix pour la candidate démocrate Mary Peltola, avec 4200 voix d'avance sur le candidat républicain sortant, Dan S. Sullivan.
Le décompte du New York Times prenait en compte, dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi, 84% des votes, toujours en cours de dépouillement.
Résultat serré
Cindy Hyde-Smith, en poste depuis 2018, a reconnu sa défaite dans une vidéo publiée sur le réseau social X.

CNN a annoncé la victoire de M. Colom mercredi, huit jours après le scrutin, en se fondant sur 99% de bulletins dépouillés, le démocrate obtenant 49,2% des voix contre 48,7% pour sa concurrente républicaine, soit seulement 4585 voix d'écart.
Scott Colom doit devenir le premier sénateur noir de cet ancien Etat confédéré depuis Blanche Bruce (1875-1881).

items.titel: What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair?
items.anriss: Nvidia says no secrets were compromised, but experts question what sensitive information may have been exposed.

absaetze.t: United States lawmakers are pushing for answers from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid growing concerns over whether an affair he had compromised national security.

Huang, 63, has admitted to having extramarital relations during his time leading Nvidia, a major US tech firm. Media reports indicate the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed who is accused of working for Chinese intelligence.

As the scandal continues to grip Washington, Republican leaders of three committees in the House of Representatives have asked Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing to testify about the relationship.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast said he was prepared to subpoena Huang if he did not respond by the end of Wednesday.

According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the Nvidia CEO and influence him to push for looser restrictions on chip sales to China.
In a statement on Sunday, Jensen Huang apologised to his family and Nvidia employees about the affair.

His company also launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe that “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised”. Still, by Wednesday, media reports emerged that Nvidia was preparing to part ways with Huang over the controversy.
US President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the matter, but he has stood by Huang, calling him an “honourable guy”.
But the pressure on Huang intensified on Tuesday when Republican Senator Kevin Cramer called for him to resign.
“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer said in an interview with Politico.
But Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago, has shown no signs of heeding that call.

Despite the company’s assurances, experts say the affair raises concerns about what information Alice Huang may have been privy to and what role the relationship may have played in the Nvidia CEO’s decisions.
What are the national security concerns surrounding Nvidia?
Nvidia’s advanced chips, which power much of today’s artificial intelligence, have put the company at the centre of the race for tech dominance between China and the US.
Since 2022, Washington has restricted sales of some of the most advanced chips to China over concerns that they could be used by the country’s military or intelligence agencies.
According to US intelligence officials cited by The New York Times, Alice Huang was tasked with getting Jensen Huang to lobby for looser restrictions on chip exports.
The Nvidia CEO had already been pushing for an easing of the rules, arguing that China’s domestic chip industry would get stronger without better access to US products.

But some experts say it is worth looking at how Alice Huang may have influenced decisions Nvidia made specifically about her former employer Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips over the span of about two years.
Megaspeed has also been investigated over allegations that it helped Chinese companies get access to restricted chips. Megaspeed denies the allegation.

Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation who studies Chinese technology and intelligence activities, pointed to reports from Bloomberg and The New York Times that Nvidia contacted the US Commerce Department about its investigation into Megaspeed.
He also noted that, in disclosures to the government, Nvidia appeared to vastly undercount the value of the chips it sold to the company.

“The question at hand is whether Nvidia took specific actions with respect to Megaspeed that it might not otherwise have done,” Fedasiuk told Al Jazeera, “possibly as a result of the personal relationship between the two executives.”
What sensitive information could have been a risk?
There are also questions about what sensitive information Alice Huang may have had access to through her relationship with Jensen Huang.
In an analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations, a think tank, senior fellow Jessica Brandt pointed to information about how Nvidia designs its China-specific chips.

“Information about its conversations with policymakers could be helpful for anticipating where those controls and other policies are headed,” she said. “Understanding where it disagrees with government could expose fault lines to exploit. And that’s before we get into anything touching R&D [research and development].”

Fedasiuk raised similar concerns about what Alice Huang could have learned about Nvidia’s internal operations and plans for future products, as well as its customer base, which includes American and foreign tech companies.
He also pointed to Jensen Huang’s close ties to Trump and other senior White House officials.
“I have to wonder what kind of information about those people and about those relationships may have inadvertently made its way to Ms Huang or to Chinese intelligence,” he said.

So far, however, there is no publicly available evidence that Alice Huang got access to sensitive information from Nvidia or influenced Jensen Huang’s decisions. US intelligence also has not made public any evidence that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence.
China has flatly denied the allegations of espionage.
“The claim of so-called ‘Chinese spies’ is completely groundless and is nothing but a smear campaign against China,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun on Monday.

items.titel: Ukraine Regretting White House-Brokered Temporary Ceasefire In Strategic Riverside Town Of Oleshky
items.anriss: Ukrainian officials are expressing major regrets about a White House-brokered temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, which sits on the Russian-held side of the Dnipro River, the body of water that serves as a dividing line between the opposing …

absaetze.t: Ukrainian officials are expressing major regrets about a White House-brokered temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, which sits on the Russian-held side of the Dnipro River, the body of water that serves as a dividing line between the opposing forces. Kyiv is concerned Russian forces will once again use this decimated locale to bombard Kherson City with cross-river drone and artillery attacks.

As many as 2,000 Ukrainian citizens were left in this town at the edge of the front line, caught between drone and artillery volleys launched by both sides. Intensive Ukrainian drone operations had largely ran the Russians out of Oleshky and a wide swath of territory as far as 30 km behind the lines, according to the Kyiv Post, citing Russian sources. This had reduced, but not prevented, Russian attacks against the Ukrainian side of the river. As we reported last year, Moscow’s forces have been carrying out widespread drone strikes on largely civilian targets in this region for quite some time in order to wear down the population, primarily in the large city of Kherson just across the river.

The military governor of the Kherson region has claimed that Russia took advantage of the ceasefire, brokered by First Lady Melania Trump to restore its forces in the bombed-out town. The statements by Oleksandr Prokudin follow comments made by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and a Ukrainian military officer that the Russians moved troops and equipment into the area under the cover of the ceasefire and will use them to step up attacks across the Dnipro.

“It took us about a year to eliminate what they have now restored during the ceasefire,” Prokudin told Ukrainian Pravda. “They have restored almost everything. They used this time very effectively: they carried out personnel rotations, rebuilt completely destroyed positions, and resupplied themselves with food, generators, and fuel.”
During the ceasefire, the Russians moved drones, artillery and ammunition into Oleshky, Prokudin stated.
“Furthermore, enemy troops searched Oleshky for basements to set up new hideouts for drone operators,” the Ukrainian official noted, adding that an increase in enemy strikes should be expected.

“Currently, the occupiers are launching approximately 700–800 drone attacks per day, deliberately terrorizing the civilian population of Kherson and the coastal communities,” he said. “They will 100% increase.”
A video of Russian forces moving back into Oleshky, which you can see below, emerged on social media on Nov. 2, the day after the ceasefire ended.
Russia has not officially commented on these claims, which TWZ cannot independently verify. We reached out to Melania Trump’s office for comment about the Ukrainian claims.
How Did The Ceasefire Come To Be?

Home to some 24,000 people before the all-out Russian invasion, Oleshky was captured as the Russians pushed toward the Dnipro River. With the city now largely in ruins after more than four years of conflict, the population, as we noted earlier in this story, had dwindled to fewer than 2,000, mostly senior citizens and children unable to get out, according to the White House. In October, First Lady Melania Trump brokered a deal that would allow many of those residents to leave.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” the First Lady said in announcing that the localized ceasefire, the first of its kind, would commence Oct. 29. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”

The First Lady and her representative “worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire,” the statement added. “The First Lady initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary.”

After several rounds of negotiations, the ceasefire ultimately began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time on Oct. 27 and ended late on Nov. 1, said Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who called it the longest such arrangement since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Lubinets and David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky’s parliamentary faction, were the Ukrainian negotiators. After the ceasefire ended, both men praised the operation and Melania Trump held a press conference at the White House to announce the results.
How The Ceasefire Worked
The operation unfolded in several stages, Lubinets said, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).

“After the cease-fire took effect, Russian forces began demining roads leading to Oleshky, a process that continued through Oct. 29,” the publication stated. “Humanitarian supplies, including food, medicine, drinking water, and specialized hospital equipment, were then delivered.”

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, accompanied by their teams and journalists from Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia, “subsequently entered the occupied city to oversee the distribution of aid and assist residents seeking evacuation,” the outlet added. “Residents were given three options: remain in Oleshky and receive humanitarian assistance, leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory, or travel to Russia or territory under Russian control.”

During this effort, the Ukrainian delegation “experimented with drone surveillance and direct communication between Ukrainian and Russian military representatives to monitor compliance,” the news outlet noted. “Arakhamia said the experience had helped demonstrate how localized cease-fires could be verified rather than relying solely on competing military intelligence claims.”

“All people who wanted to be evacuated from Oleshky to Ukraine are now in Ukraine,” Lubinets said, adding that he had “personally overseen the evacuation process and spoken with residents to establish whether their decisions were voluntary.”
Lantratova concurred that the ceasefire went off as planned in terms of the humanitarian goals.
“I can state that there were no incidents or violations of the ceasefire,” she said, according to Russian media. “Everything went exactly as planned.”
Ukraine Soon Expressed Regret
As noted earlier in this story, Ukrainian officials began to express concerns about the military results of the ceasefire about a week after it ended.
Russia brought more than 1,000 troops into the area under the cover of the ceasefire, an officer with the unit defending the Ukrainian side of the Dnipro claimed on Nov. 6.

“Russian forces have massed in positions from which they had been driven out over the past six months, effectively moving about 20 kilometers closer to the line of contact,” Yaroslav Moroz, head of the Unmanned Systems Department of the 34th Separate Marine Brigade of the Ukrainian Navy, told RFE/RL. “Prior to the ceasefire, the situation on the left bank of the Kherson region was different: the Armed Forces of Ukraine had expanded their engagement zone, pushed the enemy back, and severed their logistics.”

“There are no massive assault operations at the moment. However, we are prepared for them,” Moroz added. “Russian forces have brought a large quantity of equipment and ammunition into the Oleshky hospital, knowing that the Armed Forces of Ukraine would not attack the building, as local residents are receiving medical treatment there.”
Two days later, Zelensky complained about the Russian advances in the region.

“Unfortunately, under the cover of a humanitarian operation in Oleshky, the Russian army carried out a major rotation of personnel and equipment on the left bank,” the Ukrainian leader stated on X. “Additional occupation forces were brought into Oleshky and the surrounding community. The command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine must present proposals for additional protection of lives in Kherson from Russian terror.”

Ukrainian officials took the calculated risk that making a deal with Russia would benefit a large number of people caught in the middle of a brutal conflict. After what Ukrainians claimed transpired following the ceasefire, the future of such endeavors is unclear.

items.titel: Plans To Fly Talon Blue CCA Drone From British Carrier Confirmed By Northrop Grumman
items.anriss: The Royal Navy is aiming to see Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) drone fly from a British aircraft carrier next year. The planned demonstration is another notable step toward a carrier-based CCA capability …

absaetze.t: The Royal Navy is aiming to see Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) drone fly from a British aircraft carrier next year. The planned demonstration is another notable step toward a carrier-based CCA capability in the United Kingdom. The plans also signal significant new opportunities on the horizon for Talon Blue, the first flight of which was only announced last month.

“We look forward to working with the Royal Navy over the next 12 months on this future demonstration,” Northrop Grumman told TWZ in a statement today. “Thursday’s signing is an important step in demonstrating relevant British naval capabilities, building on Northrop Grumman’s decades of leadership in autonomy and commitment to mission-relevant platforms and systems.”

First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins had first announced plans to launch Talon Blue, which the U.S. military has also designated the YFQ-48A, from a carrier during an address yesterday at the International Sea Power Conference in Norway. Jenkins, the first Royal Marine to ever hold the post of First Sea Lord, the United Kingdom’s top naval officer, made his remarks aboard the HMS Prince of Wales. That ship is the second of two Queen Elizabeth class carriers in Royal Navy service today.

“In two days’ time, on this carrier, I will sign a statement of intent with our friends at Northrop Grumman to prepare their Talon demonstrator for trials with the Royal Navy under Project Vanquish,” Jenkins declared to those in attendance. “Through that agreement, we will work towards a demonstration in U.K. waters in 2027, including a launch from the carrier.”

The planned tests involving Talon “will give us the evidence we need to understand how uncrewed combat aircraft can operate safely and effectively alongside the existing air wing. Then we learn, adapt and keep moving forward,” he continued. “That is how we deliver capability at the pace necessary. Not by waiting years for a perfect solution, but by working with industry to get the latest technology into the hands of our people as quickly as possible. Of course, moving at pace carries some risk.”

Jenkins first announced Project Vanquish in September 2025. As outlined then, the project’s goal was to demonstrate the ability to launch and recover what authorities in the U.K. refer to as a Tier 2 Autonomous Collaborative Platform (ACP) from a carrier without the need for a catapult or arresting gear. The Royal Navy’s Queen Elizabeth class carriers are so-called short-takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) types that lack catapults and arresting gear, but there has been talk in the past about adding those features in some form down the line.

In the British government’s parlance, Tier 2 ACPs are defined primarily by being ‘attritable.’ This, in turn, is generally taken to mean designs that are low-cost enough to be employed in higher-risk environments from which they may not return, but that are also capable enough to conduct relevant missions.

Since Talon Blue was first officially disclosed in December 2025, at a media event that TWZ attended, Northrop Grumman has talked about the design as being lower-cost. However, the company does not appear to have used attritable or similar terms to describe the drone. Hard cost data of any kind has yet to be disclosed. Talon Blue does appear to be in line, broadly speaking, with the complexity of the two CCAs now in production for the U.S. Air Force. Those drones, General Atomics FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril’s FQ-44A Fury, are understood to have unit costs in the low tens of millions

“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness,” Craig Woolston, Vice President and General Manager for Research and Advanced Design, at Northrop Grumman said in a statement accompanying the announcement of Talon Blue’s maiden flight last month. “We listened. Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities. Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”

What it might take to configure Talon Blue for carrier-based operations remains to be seen, even without the need for the drone to be capable of catapult launches and arrested recoveries. An entirely new variant could well be required, if it is not already in the works.

It should be noted that the Royal Navy has already demonstrated the ability to launch and recover several different types of propeller-driven drones from the decks of its Queen Elizabeth class carriers since 2023. This includes the Mojave from General Atomics in the United States. Just earlier this month, the service announced that the Tekever AR5 had joined this list. The British Army is already in the process of acquiring AR5s for land-based use to replace its long-troubled Watchkeeper drones. None of these drones are as advanced as the jet-powered Talon Blue.
The Royal Navy has also launched other smaller drones, including long-range one-way-attack types, from its Queen Elizabeth class carriers via trailer-mounted catapults in the past.

All of this has been in sevice of a broader Royal Navy push to incorporate more uncrewed platforms with higher degrees of autonomy into its operations in the air and at sea. The service has dubbed this broader vision as its Hybrid Navy concept.

“I do not believe the Royal Navy can build the Hybrid Navy at the speed we need it by doing things the way we have always done,” First Sea Lord Jenkins said yesterday, speaking about these plans more broadly. “During my career, I have seen too many examples of what happens when institutions become too set in their ways. So I need industry alongside us from the start.”

The decision to involve Northrop Grumman Talon Blue also represents a significant development for that drone. The company has said the genesis behind this uncrewed aircraft was lessons learned from its failed bid in the first phase, or Increment 1, of the U.S. Air Force’s CCA program. Especially since it received its U.S. military designation, Talon Blue has looked well positioned for the Air Force’s follow-on Increment 2 CCA competition.

Northrop Grumman is also one of the companies under contract now to develop a conceptual carrier-based CCA design for the U.S. Navy. The company has yet to share details about what that proposed drone might look like, but a demonstration of Talon Blue operating from a British carrier could provide hints.

The market space for land- and carrier-based CCAs has also expanded globally. Talon Blue is just one of several notable new designs to break cover in this arena in recent years, including in the United Kingdom. This development trend also extends to potential adversaries, and China in particular.

The CCA market could be differently important for Northrop Grumman going forward given the company’s recent loss to Boeing in the U.S. Navy’s F/A-XX next-generation carrier-based fighter competition. Back in 2023, Northrop Grumman had also dropped out of the running for the U.S. Air Force competition that led to the F-47, which is also being built by Boeing. Northrop Grumman is the prime contractor for a number of other very high-profile U.S. military programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and the LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM).

Plans to launch Talon Blue from a British carrier are still very much in their infancy, but the demonstration now on the horizon for next year looks set to be an important development for all parties involved.

items.titel: France’s supermarket fridges might be thawing but the country’s relationship with Iran is ice cold
items.anriss: Who vs who: France vs Iran What it’s about: Several rubbish dumps’ worth of melted Roquefort, mouldering pâté and spoiled quiche ( writes Andrew Mueller ). Last month the software for hundreds of supermarket fridges in France – and …

absaetze.t: What it’s about: Several rubbish dumps’ worth of melted Roquefort, mouldering pâté and spoiled quiche (writes Andrew Mueller). Last month the software for hundreds of supermarket fridges in France – and elsewhere – was hacked, raising their temperatures and ruining their contents. France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (Anssi) determined that this was the work of a hacker cell known as Shahid Kaveh, which is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The French Foreign Ministry summoned Iran’s ambassador in Paris to formally express its displeasure. It sounds as though it would have been a meeting without éclairs anyway: the French Foreign Ministry has the excuse that few refrigerated treats were available.

What it’s really about: France believes – and not implausibly – that it has been the target of Iranian hybrid warfare, for which Iran has long-standing form in Europe and elsewhere. The fridge-hacking bears all the hallmarks of a classic hybrid-warfare operation. It’s expensive and bewildering to the target, cheap and effective to the perpetrator, and has the added bonus of being readily deniable. And indeed, Iran denies it, harrumphing that France’s charge is “baseless and malicious”, part of a “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against Iran”.

Likely resolution: France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has vowed “necessary and proportionate” measures by way of retaliation, though it is hard to imagine what these might be, unless he has instructed Anssi to do its worst to Iranian ice creameries. The EU, which has also pledged a “swift and united” response, can no doubt impose further sanctions on Iran, though it is difficult to imagine that the IRGC would care much. In hybrid warfare, the attacker has some enraging advantages, especially when it is waging its campaign on a democratic country – there is always a vulnerability somewhere.

absaetze.t: Candle wax drips onto the holder and the last trickle of wine is poured out between glasses, before another bottle is uncorked. A window is opened and an icy breeze seeps in. People are picking at the cheese board, while others linger in the corridor, rapt in conversation. The sound of talking fills every inch of the room. Then there’s the familiar plink of piano keys. Someone at the party has requested a song. As it becomes clear which carol has been chosen, everyone gathers around to start singing. Arms are slung over shoulders and suddenly a cacophony of voices becomes one.

This is often the way that soirées end when I visit my friends who own a piano. In the city, having such an instrument is rare because of space restrictions and poor sound insulation. But we know that when we come here, there’s a good chance that this is where the evening will lead. I have known these particular friends since childhood and both are musically inclined – one now does it professionally. I have spent many hours singing with them in choirs, on school buses and at concerts over the years. We have grown up together, played together, made mistakes together, become ourselves together. Singing with them feels natural. It would feel odd if we didn’t do it any more.

At their dinner parties, there are usually a handful of guests I’ve never met before, who didn’t see me navigate adolescence disgracefully like our hosts did. But by the end of the night, we’re all throwing our hands in the air, riotously belting “five gold rings” when the moment comes in “The Twelve Days of Christmas”, and we too are now bonded. It’s the “ice-breaker effect” of singing, as one Oxford study called it. We sing longer when it’s spontaneous, going through all of the old favourites until the small hours. This pursuit isn’t reserved for the wintertime. Beyond festivities, we gravitate towards anything from Squeeze’s “Tempted” to Ivor Novello’s “We’ll Gather Lilacs”, depending on whether the mood calls for 1980s pop-rock or wartime anthems. But at this time of year, there are myriad songs from which to choose that are universal. Christmas is one of those rare times when everyone, whether religious or not, can join in and sing. The festive repertoire is wonderfully forgiving: its melodies tend to be memorable, its rhythms clear, its refrains repetitive. You can arrive halfway through and still find your way in.

There’s something truly cathartic about singing in a group in this way. It feels good to allow your voice to travel out, to feel your lungs fill and empty, your ribs expand, your throat open. Singing together forces everyone to breathe to the same rhythm. The vagus nerve, which is directly connected to the vocal cords, puts the nervous system into a relaxed state and controlled exhalation releases endorphins – related to pleasure and feelings of wellbeing – as well as strengthening your heart.

Singing in a choir has been studied as a way to enhance quality of life for those with various health conditions. Notably, researchers have found that it improves the ability of Parkinson’s patients to articulate and it helps to prompt memories in those with dementia. Also, you connect in real time with those around you, which is increasingly difficult in the digital age.

Many evolutionary biologists and psychologists believe that singing predates formal language. It is arguably a more immediate way to connect with others than with words alone. There’s evidence from the Upper Palaeolithic period (which began about 50,000 years ago) that suggests that early humans gathered around fires to sing, orally passing down traditions to successive generations. Even now, with developed language at our disposal, singing can help us to bond more effectively than speech. A 2022 US study found that it produced greater positive feelings for choir members than conversing with one another, with an increased sense of social connectedness.

In modern history, singing has been a tool of solidarity – think of the spirituals sung on US plantations to provide hope and unite people during the dark times of slavery. Sailors in the age of exploration sang sea shanties to help synchronise labour. And then there’s the singing that happens in places of worship: united, liberated, whole-bodied. Such environments have been a fertile training ground for some of the world’s greatest vocalists. Aretha Franklin, Elvis Presley, Sam Cooke, Luciano Pavarotti and Patsy Cline all spent their childhoods singing in churches.

The best singers are not necessarily those with the best instruments but those who warble unselfconsciously and from the heart – something that being part of a choir facilitates. For most people, standing alone on a stage and singing a tune takes courage: they need to prepare mentally, calm their nerves and find a way to lean into the performance. But stand shoulder to shoulder beside others tackling the same song and the weight is gone. All that’s left is the joy of it. If your voice wobbles, there are many other voices to catch it. If you come in late, somebody else is already carrying the phrase. Sociologist Émile Durkheim coined the term “collective effervescence” to describe the sacred, electric joy that happens when a community moves and sings together. You become something larger than yourself, more than an individual, and feel the underlying happiness of being human.

So, every December, these melodies resurface from hymn books, old recordings and our memories. Some date back hundreds of years; some are sentimental or spiritual; many are ridiculous (see “We Wish You a Merry Christmas”, in which the carollers begin demanding figgy pudding and refuse to leave until they get some). But therein lies the charm. When the last chord is played, glasses are topped up – and it’s on to the next.

The news came in a press release ahead of New York's marquee auction week, promising interested budding criminals users an exclusive opportunity to “trade yes-or-no contracts in a peer-to-peer structure” (??) on public art sales. The mechanism is as follows: Artnet will use its Price Database, once nostalgically the realm of wannabe art advisors trying to sound like they have an MBA, to “curate" (help) “events” (HELP) such as whether a lot will exceed its estimate. Surprising no one, Miami Art Week in December will be the “next major moment” for the partnership, bro.

absaetze.t: The best part of the new documentary about the famed artist is watching people interact with his work.
November 11, 2026 — 2 min read

A new documentary about Romare Bearden embraces a collage-like sensibility, fitting well with the artist’s most influential work. Romare Bearden: A Life in Collage, soon to screen at DOC NYC, eschews the familiar structure of a linear biography, jumping around to find thematic rhymes through different periods of Bearden’s life.
Early on, for instance, the film alludes to Bearden’s family’s participation in the Great Migration, but rather than dwell on his biography, it turns to the recurring motif of trains in his work.

The film benefits from generous access to recordings of Bearden himself, who speaks with remarkable elegance about his memories, artistic process, and influences. Shaped by living in the South, Harlem, and Pittsburgh, his studies at the Sorbonne, and his time in the military and semiprofessional baseball during the first half of the 20th century, Bearden synthesized them into an oeuvre now seen as emblematic of the broader Black experience of the era.
